## Why white-tailed deer?

White-tailed deer (sek̓wtúps) are expanding north into the Columbia Mountains around Revelstoke, BC, into valleys that once had deeper snow and older forest. That matters for southern mountain caribou, which are threatened and among the southernmost caribou in the world. More deer can support more wolves and cougars, and more predators can mean more caribou killed, even when predators mostly hunt deer. This is called apparent competition. Deer can also spread chronic wasting disease (CWD), a fatal disease of deer, elk, moose, and caribou.

To protect caribou, wolves, cougars, and moose have been reduced across parts of the region. That buys caribou time, but it may also open the door for deer. My M.Sc. asks where deer are expanding, how they use the landscape across seasons and elevations, and what is driving it.

## Study area

More than 7,000 km² of the Columbia Mountains, from valley bottoms near 400 m to alpine ridges above 3,000 m. It spans private land, provincial Crown land, and federally protected national parks, each with its own history of logging, roads, and predator management.

## A shared camera network

More than 200 trail cameras deployed since 2019 record deer alongside a full community of large mammals, including eight mid-to-large predators and seven ungulates, and millions of images have been tagged. The cameras come from Parks Canada, Biodiversity Pathways, and Splatsin. Pooling them into one dataset made this question answerable, and working with these partners has been one of the best parts of this project.

## Preliminary results

::: {.prelim}
**These results are preliminary.** The analysis is still being finalized, and these numbers and interpretations may change.
:::

- **Deer are becoming more common.** On the 48 cameras watched every year from 2020 to 2024, the share of sites with white-tailed deer doubled, from about 19% to 38%.
- **Summer visitors to the high country, valley residents in winter.** Deer use mid and high elevations in the snow-free months. In six winters of monitoring, not one was recorded above the valley bottom.
- **Cold, snow, and rugged terrain matter most.** Temperature, snow water equivalent (SWE, how much water the snowpack holds), and terrain ruggedness best explained where deer were: they were scarcest where it was coldest, snowiest, and most rugged.
- **No clear predator effect, yet.** Wolves and cougars were photographed so rarely (wolves on 114 of nearly 195,000 camera-days) that an effect can't be ruled out.
- **Still a minority animal.** White-tailed deer showed up on about 1% of camera-days, roughly half as often as moose or mule deer. People made up 42% of all detections.
